summary:
Kogi State stands under Nigeria's national framework. The Same Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2013, passed by the House of Representatives on 30 May 2013 and signed into law in January 2014, applies in Kogi in full: entering a same-sex marriage or civil union carries 14 years' imprisonment, and registering, operating or participating in gay clubs, societies and organisations, or making a public show of a same-sex amorous relationship, carries 10 years.

Kogi is administered under secular law rather than Shari'a. It is one of the states outside the twelve Shari'a-administering northern states, so the federal 14-year maximum applies to same-sex conduct there and the death penalties applied in northern states such as Kano and Katsina do not reach a visitor in Kogi.

The Criminal Code separately criminalises sex between men with up to 14 years' imprisonment and gross indecency with up to 3 years' imprisonment.

In 2022 a coalition of Nigerian human rights organisations won a court ruling that Sections 4(1), 5(2) and 5(3) of the 2013 Act breached the Constitution and could not be enforced anywhere in the country, which effectively allows LGBTQ+ organisations and individuals to exist and organise, including in Kogi. The ruling does not extend to the conduct and marriage-prohibition provisions of the Act, which remain enforceable.

Nigeria's Constitution contains no specific protections on the basis of sexual orientation, and there are no federal anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people. A visitor in Kogi therefore has no statutory protection against discrimination in accommodation, services or employment.

Mass arrests and detention of LGBTQ+ people are common across Nigeria, including in Kogi, and are recorded as especially frequent in northern states.
tangentialFactors:
The best-documented killing of a transgender person in Nigeria during this period occurred outside Kogi. BBC News (9 August 2024) reported that the body of the transgender TikToker known as 'Abuja Area Mama', aged 33, was found on a highway in Abuja, beaten to death; police opened an investigation, and she had been stabbed a year earlier and had feared for her life. The case illustrates the level of violence and the official response a trans person may face, but the incident itself took place in Abuja, not Kogi.

The concentration of documented enforcement in northern states is a matter of jurisdictional geography rather than a Kogi finding: the twelve Shari'a-administering states impose harsher penalties, with death penalties applied in Kano and Katsina for lesbianism, while non-Shari'a states such as Kogi sit under the federal 14-year maximum. A comparison of penalties between states therefore reflects which legal regime administers them, not a difference in the underlying national statute.

The 2022 constitutional ruling is national in scope and was won by a domestic coalition rather than by any Kogi institution; it removes enforcement of the organisational provisions of the 2013 Act countrywide while leaving its conduct and marriage provisions intact everywhere, Kogi included.
localsOnly:
Residents of Kogi live under the federal 14-year maximum for same-sex conduct, with no Shari'a layer applied locally and no local statute of their own addressing same-sex relations.

The 2022 court ruling applies within Kogi: Sections 4(1), 5(2) and 5(3) of the 2013 Act are unenforceable, so LGBTQ+ organisations and individuals may exist and organise in the state, and no comparable ruling protects the conduct or marriage provisions.

Kogi residents have no constitutional protection on the basis of sexual orientation and no federal anti-discrimination protection, and mass arrests and detention of LGBTQ+ people are recorded as occurring in Kogi as well as elsewhere in Nigeria.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Kogi-specific court case, charge, conviction or named incident involving a transgender or LGBTQ person was identified in the sources provided. The only incident in the inventory, the killing of 'Abuja Area Mama', occurred in Abuja and is carried here as context, not as a Kogi event.

The sources do not state how many arrests for same-sex conduct have been made in Kogi specifically, how many were made in other states, or over what period, so the claim that mass detention occurs 'including in Kogi' cannot be quantified here. Arrest figures cited elsewhere in the parent record are counts by state with no per-capita denominator.

Whether the 2022 ruling has been invoked in proceedings within Kogi, and whether any Kogi court has applied the unenforced sections, is not sourced. Nor is there sourced information on the availability of trans-specific healthcare, gender-affirming documentation practice, or police complaint handling in Kogi.
